summary: Gives a problem statement and requirements for managing networks that include constrained devices, such as small, low-power, low-memory nodes. It also sketches deployment and management topology options. It is background for work on management protocols, not a protocol.

eli5.summary: Tiny gadgets with little memory still need looking after. This lists the problems and what an overseer system must handle to care for them.

subtitle: Why managing networks of tiny, battery-powered devices is different, and a catalogue of what a management system should handle.

tldr.problem: Constrained devices have limited CPU, memory and energy and often sit on lossy or sleepy links, so the management protocols built for ordinary IP networks do not fit them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes network types, deployment and management topologies, configuration and monitoring levels, and a problem statement, then lists requirements grouped into eleven management areas with type and priority for each.
tldr.outcome: It is background material and a set of objectives for discussion, not a protocol, and it deliberately does not make any requirement mandatory.

today: RFC 7547 is an Informational document, published in May 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its use cases are in RFC 7548.

sections.title: Why Constrained Devices Need Their Own Management
sections.content:
Constrained devices (also called sensors, smart objects or smart devices) have limited CPU, memory and power. They may sit on unreliable or lossy channels, use wireless technologies with limited bandwidth and a dynamic topology, or reach the Internet through a gateway or proxy. The RFC expects the Internet of Things to grow to trillions of such devices over the next decade.

Network management means monitoring status, detecting faults and inferring causes, setting parameters and acting to keep things running. Constrained devices may be unreliable, short on power and left in harsh environments for a long time, so the usual approach does not carry over. The RFC says the IETF had so far developed no specific technologies for managing them, and that devices were using application-layer protocols in an ad hoc manner.

The document gives a problem statement and a list of requirements, and builds its terms on RFC 7228. Use cases are in RFC 7548. It does not aim to be a strict requirements document, because no single solution is likely to suit all use cases.
sections.eli5: Normal computers can be checked on all day. Tiny battery gadgets sleep a lot and cannot talk much, so the caretaker has to be gentler.

sections.title: Networks and Topologies in Focus
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes four network types: wireline unconstrained networks such as Ethernet, mixed wireline and wireless networks with multi-hop dynamic routing, mixed networks with point-to-point or point-to-multipoint links and often a single hop, and self-configuring infrastructureless networks of mobile devices such as MANETs. It mentions 6LoWPAN (RFC 4919) and RPL (RFC 6550) on top of IEEE 802.15.4 as ways to get multi-hop connectivity.

Networks are further described by topology, how often the topology changes, traffic flows, bandwidth and loss rate. For example, wired loss rates are typically around 10^-12 or 10^-13 for 10 Gbit Ethernet, while IEEE 802.15.4 can reach 10^-1 to 1 under interference. Very static networks, with changes less than once every 30 minutes, are in scope if they carry constrained devices.

Devices can be deployed in a network of their own, directly on an IP network, behind a gateway or proxy, or in a hierarchy from C0 devices up through C1 and C2 devices to gateways and servers. Management can be one central manager (possibly hierarchical), distributed across several managers, or hierarchical by network level.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets live on a calm wired street and some on a noisy wireless one where messages get lost. The caretaker must plan for both kinds of street.

sections.title: Constrainedness and Management Levels
sections.content:
The RFC lists how a device or network can be constrained and what each constraint means for management. A device might support only a lossy link, wake up only from time to time, have a limited operating time, support only one simple protocol, support little or no security, or talk to only one managing entity. A network might need multicast configuration, have 10,000 or more nodes, need self-organization, or need energy-efficient management that uses as little wireless bandwidth as possible.

It also defines scales for what devices can do. Configuration levels run from CL0 (preconfigured, no runtime changes) to CL6 (configuration change transactions across devices). Monitoring levels run from ML0 (device pushes predefined data) to ML3 (device processes data locally to detect thresholds or aggregate). At the time of writing, constrained devices often combined one of CL0 to CL2 with one of ML0 or ML1.
sections.eli5: Gadgets can be grouped by how much they can be told to change and how much they can report. A very simple one only does what it was built to do and just sends occasional news.

sections.title: The Problem Statement
sections.content:
Constrained nodes force a rethink of protocol characteristics in terms of power consumption, performance, bandwidth, memory and CPU usage. The IETF was already developing protocols such as CoAP (RFC 7252) for constrained communication, but with many devices, in some scenarios up to a million, easy deployment, configuration and management become important, as does self-configuration, which often needs device-initiated connection setup.

In an ideal world there would be one management protocol for monitoring, configuration and data exchange across network types, with basic data models derived from the core models used today. The RFC says current management protocols seem too heavyweight to apply directly to constrained devices, and that data models for them still needed to be designed. It questions whether the comprehensive IP network approach can be reused, and concludes management here is necessarily simplified.
sections.eli5: The big, heavy tools for looking after normal computers are too much for a tiny gadget. We need lighter tools made for them.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
Requirements are grouped into eleven areas: management architecture, management protocols and data models, configuration management, monitoring, self-management, security and access control, energy management, software distribution, traffic management, transport layer, and implementation. Each one has a Req-ID, title, description, source use case, a functional or non-functional type, the device classes (C0, C1, C2) that can support it, and a priority of High, Medium or Low.

Examples from the architecture area include supporting multiple device classes in one network (1.001), scalability through caching, in-network aggregation and hierarchical management, minimizing state kept on devices, eventual consistency after devices were offline, and not assuming that devices are always reachable (1.006). The management system must also cope with devices that sleep or have lossy links.

The RFC is explicit that the requirements are separated from their context and that it does not recommend implementing any particular subset or make any of them mandatory. An implementer or vendor may choose a relevant subset.
sections.eli5: It is a long wish list for the caretaker system, sorted into topics like energy, security and updates. Nobody has to grant every wish, they pick the ones that matter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Constrained devices are often placed in unsafe environments where attackers can reach them physically. The RFC says devices should be robust and tamper resistant, have no backdoors, offer no non-essential services and protect stored credentials. Credentials leaking from one device should not make attacks on similar devices easier, and credentials should never be shared.

Cryptographic algorithms should be efficient yet strong, and long-lived devices need algorithms that can be updated after deployment. The ability to perform secure firmware and software updates is called an important management requirement. Sensitive data should be protected, including while it is cached or stored in a store-and-forward transport. The detailed security requirements are in Section 3.6 (authentication, bootstrapping, access control and efficient cryptography).
sections.eli5: Little gadgets are often left out where anyone could grab them. They need good locks that are not too heavy for them, and each gadget needs its own key.

items.label: Preconfigured
items.desc: No runtime configuration changes; often hard coded in firmware.

items.label: Explicit objects
items.desc: Configuration objects exist, but changes need a restart.

items.label: Bulk replacement
items.desc: Whole configuration or subsets replaced; takes effect by soft restart.

items.label: Per-object changes
items.desc: Objects modified without bulk replacement; effective immediately.

items.label: Multiple datastores
items.desc: Distinguishes running from next startup configuration.

items.label: Locking and transactions
items.desc: Datastore locking and device-local change transactions, all or none.

items.label: Pull
items.desc: Management system pulls predefined monitoring data.

items.label: Filtered pull
items.desc: Management system pulls user-defined filtered subsets.

items.label: Local processing
items.desc: Device detects threshold crossings or aggregates data locally.
